We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

A 3D human anatomy application built with @threejs using GPT 5.6 Sol. It all started with a single design image that I created using GPT Image 2.0. I then used it to generate every 3D organ image, one by one. Next, I converted each of those images into 3D models using @tripoai (and no, they didn't sponsor this 😄). Codex built the first version beautifully, but there was one big problem. Every single 3D model was nearly 120-150 MB. That obviously wasn't practical for the web and was giving a performance of 16fps. After a few iterations, Codex optimized each model down to roughly 2–5.5 MB while preserving the visual quality, reducing the total asset size from ~900 MB to just 28.6 MB. And each model loads on demand. Along the way, Codex also generated those anatomical illustrations showing where each organ sits in the human body, and even created the interactive hotspot markers that explain different parts of every organ. It handled all of that. The process wasn't exactly one shot, but it also wasn't difficult. You just have to do it step by step. It genuinely felt like building something that could make learning anatomy much more engaging. The inspiration came from @DilumSanjaya 's 3D animal plant cell project. If you want to join an ambitious and pragmatic AI safety team, you should get in touch :) Alex Robey (@AlexRobey23) 1/ There's not a clear one-size-fits-all formula for open-weight releases. Each release should weigh a bunch of things: dual-use capabilities, how robust safeguards are (e.g., to fine-tuning attacks), accessibility (cost/infra/etc.), and the overall ecosystem. Any future model release will need to evolve the criteria as models improve. 2/ Can dangerous and general capabilities be decoupled? Unclear in general, but likely answerable per domain. For biosecurity, filtering seems promising: harm is tied to specific empirical knowledge (protocols, conditions, etc.) that may be harder to rederive. For cyber, filtering seems harder: dangerous capability largely rides on reasoning + coding. 3/ There's a ton of research to do. One thing I'm excited about is adversarial fine-tuning as capability measurement. We know refusals can be stripped (abliteration, jailbreaks, etc.). The harder question is how one can measure worst-case capabilities, i.e., what can an adversarial user truly elicit (as a function of data/compute/effort)? — https://nitter.net/AlexRobey23/status/2083341332370878765#m

Inkling Small is an open weights reasoning model with 276B total parameters (12B active MoE), text, image, and speech input, and a 256K token context window. Key results: ➤ Inkling Small holds a similar tier of intelligence to Inkling’s at less than one third of its size: 276B total parameters (12B active) vs. 975B (41B active) for Inkling. No open weights model at its size or smaller scores higher on the Intelligence Index. DeepSeek V4 Flash (max), at a similar size of 284B total (13B active) also scores 40, MiniMax-M3 reaches 44 with 23B active, while GLM-5.2 (max) reaches 51 with 40B active. ➤ Inkling Small meets or exceeds Inkling on several coding and frontier reasoning evaluations. It scores higher on Humanity's Last Exam (32% vs. 30%), GPQA Diamond (89% vs. 87%), CritPt (8% vs. 5%), and SciCode (49% vs. 46%), and achieves the same score on Terminal Bench v2.1 (55%). ➤ Inkling Small is not as strong as Inkling on Agentic tasks and factual knowledge. Inkling Small trails Inkling on τ³-Banking (15% vs. 24%), though it edges ahead on GDPval-AA v2 (1269 vs. 1237 Elo). On the AA-Omniscience Index it scores -9 vs. the flagship's positive 2, meaning incorrect answers outweigh correct ones; this is driven by lower AA-Omniscience Accuracy (31% vs. 40%) rather than hallucination: Inkling Small’s Hallucination Rate is slightly lower than its larger sibling (57% vs. 63%). ➤ Inkling Small averaged ~24K output tokens per Intelligence Index task, slightly fewer than Inkling (~25K), while peers at its intelligence level averaged far more. DeepSeek V4 Flash averaged ~45K and GPT-5.4 mini (xhigh) ~78K. Running the full Intelligence Index took roughly the same number of output tokens for Inkling Small and Inkling. Mathematics and computing have had a very tight relationship in some corners of academia. Richard Courant proposed methods to solve PDEs numerically in 1928. Von Neuman figured out you could use electronic computers for it in 1940. Both were mathematicians. These methods are the ancestors of finite element methods, for which NYU's Courant Institute is famous. The Courant Institute was created in 1935 as NYU's mathematics department. It was unusual in that there was a lot of work on numerical analysis and scientific computing, with heavy use of supercomputers. In 1952, the Atomic Energy Commission installed a powerful electronic computer at NYU, which led to the creation of the Courant Mathematics and Computing Laboratory. The computer science department was spun off from mathematics in 1969 by Jacob T Schwartz. Courant is now a school with three departments: mathematics, computer science, and data science. The continued existence of an HPC center at NYU is one factor that enabled AI research to take off.

However, long term, it is simply inevitable that AI will move to patch (2). François Chollet (@fchollet) There are essentially two main options to remedy this: 1. Find ways to perform active inference, so that the model adapts its learned program in contact with a new data distribution at test time. Would likely lead to some meaningful progress, but it isn't the ultimate solution, more of an incremental improvement. 2. Change the training mechanism to something more robust than SGD, such as the MDL principle. New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents. Skills you'll gain: - Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck - Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals - Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively My teams use Cerebras for several applications that are latency sensitive. Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m

Yes, LLM architectures are getting a little more complicated

The Kimi K3 architecture figure for yesterday's big open-weight model release, along with some observations and thoughts. 1. Yes, it looks relatively complicated, but it's essentially a scaled-up production version of their Kimi Linear model they released last year (scaled up from 48B -> 2.8T; K3 is by far the biggest open-weight model right now) 2. The one new component compared to Kimi Linear is the LatentMoE. I omitted it in the figure below since it's already very crowded, but that's essentially the same LatentMoE as in Nemotron 3 Ultra (you can find it in my LLM Architecture Gallery if you are curious). The idea here is to compress (down-project) large linear layers similar to multi-head latent attention. 3. Kimi K3's overall trend (similar to Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4, and others) is also towards better inference efficiency. That is, there are many components that replace existing components with efficiency-tweaked versions. I.e., MoE -> LatentMoE, regular attention -> multi-head latent attention and Kimi Delta Attention. (I also have short tutorials and write-ups in my gallery if you are curious about additional details). 4. The one component change that is not an efficiency tweak is attention residuals. Like DeepSeek V4 improved the residual path with mHC (manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections), attention residuals are a way to improve the residual path, but it works a bit differently. I.e., mHC made the residual path wider. Attention residuals (also already part of Kimi Linear) connect the residuals across layers; the connection itself uses an attention score for an important/contribution weight. According to the report, it improves the validation loss and downstream performance (a bit) consistently and adds about 4% in training cost and 2% in inference cost. 5. Interestingly, Kimi K3 got rid of all RoPE layers and uses NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) everywhere instead. (Again, this is inherited from Kimi Linear). In other architectures, the recent trend was towards RoPE in local attention layers (like sliding window attention) and NoPE in the global layers. There were a few architectures that only used NoPE everywhere, but this is the first frontier-level one as far as I know. 6. Kimi K3 now also has native multimodal support, which is great! There are several other interesting training tidbits in the technical report, but that's it from the architecture front so far. A really great release overall.

The UK’s @AISecurityInst (AISI) has published a report on their recent cybersecurity evaluation of Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. The models attempted to complete an assignment in a setup where their normal safeguards were removed and they were deliberately given internet access. AISI reports that the models “engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations”. We’re grateful to AISI for their leadership in the important discussion about how to evaluate increasingly capable AI agents. We’re working closely with them to gather more details of the incident as we conduct our own investigation. Gaining a clear picture of Claude’s understanding of its situation—by examining its reasoning transcripts and running our own analyses—will help us identify the causes of its behavior. Here are my Opus 4.5 thoughts after ~2 weeks of use. First some general thoughts, then some practical stuff. --- THE BIG PICTURE --- THE UNLOCK FOR AGENTS It's clear to anyone who's used Opus 4.5 that AI progress isn't slowing down. I'm surprised more people aren't treating this as a major moment. I suspect getting released right before Thanksgiving combined with everyone at NeurIPS this week has delayed discourse on it by 2 weeks. But this is the best model for both code and for agents, and it's not close. The analogy has been made that this is another 3.5 Sonnet moment, and I agree. But what does that mean? Every few generations we get a major model unlock - a moment that unlocks a new way of working. GPT-4 was the unlock for chat, Sonnet 3.5 was the unlock for code, and now Opus 4.5 is the unlock for agents. Thanks to Opus 4.5, agents can now work reliably on increasingly longer time horizons and get real-world work done on your behalf. Opus 4.5 is like a Waymo. You tell it "take me from A to B", and it takes you there. After a few of these experiences your brain realizes "oh. ok. we live in this world now". And then you're hooked. From that moment on, you'll never work the same way again. THE YEAR OF AGENTS 2025 has been touted as the year of agents, and Opus 4.5 + Claude Agent SDK is the pairing that makes that phrase true. The Claude Agent SDK is the best open secret in AI right now. An agent's harness matters almost as much as its model. If you have a bad harness, then you may as well have a bad model. With the SDK you get a world-class agentic harness out-of-the-box which you can now pair with Opus 4.5 to build real-world agents that actually work. I'm reminded of Alan Kay's quote "People who are really serious about software should make their own hardware". The agent version of this is "people who are serious about models should make their own harness". Anthropic clearly believes this, and it's working. The pairing of these tools is magic. I would describe myself as being "unhobblings-pilled", and the Claude Agent SDK + Opus 4.5 is the next major unhobbling. There's now another OOM of new latent economic value stuck in this combo, and it's the job of builders to get it out. If you were bearish on agents, now is the time to turn bullish. "ALL OF THIS IS REAL" "You know what's crazy? That all of this is real". This was Ilya's opening line about the state of AI in his Dwarkesh interview, and I echo that sentiment. I can't believe that Opus 4.5 is real. There have been several times as Opus 4.5's been working where I've quite literally leaned back in my chair and given an audible laugh over how wild it is that we live in a world where it exists and where agents are this good. Nat Friedman has this great question on his website: "Where do you get your dopamine?" Increasingly, I get mine from Claude. LONG ANTHROPIC I saw a post yesterday where someone said that Opus 4.5 was the most important thing to happen to them in their professional career. This will be true for more people going forward. Every year for the past 3 years, Anthropic has grown revenue by 10x. $1M to $100M in 2023, $100M to $1B in 2024, and $1B to $10B in 2025. In Dario's recent DealBook interview he expressed that he wasn't sure if that 10x pattern would hold for 2026. While he's probably right, I do expect Anthropic's revenue at the end of next year to be much higher than everyone expects. It wouldn't surprise me if they passed OpenAI in valuation by early 2027. Opus 4.5 is too good of a model, Claude Agent SDK is too good of a harness, and their focus on the enterprise is too obviously correct. Claude Opus 4.5 is a winner. And Anthropic will keep winning.

Reminder to go touch grass A scientist in Japan demonstrated that the air inside a forest strengthens your immune system for a full month The study is incredibly fascinating: Qing Li, an immunologist at Nippon Medical School in Tokyo, took 12 men on a 3-day forest trip. These were slow walks with no breathing exercises and no set route. Then he tested their blood and found a surge in natural killer cells -- the immune cells your body uses to fight cancer and virus-infected cells. Remarkably, the effect didn't fade when they went home, it was still measurable 30 days later. A control group that walked the same distance through a city showed no change at all. Pine, cedar, and cypress trees release compounds called phytoncides to defend themselves from insects and bacteria. You breathe them in, and Li believes they switch your immune cells into high gear. He estimates one forest walk a month may be enough to keep those cells elevated all year. The best medicine might not even need a prescription -- just a walk among the trees.

@Kimi_Moonshot built a 2.8 trillion parameter model that would need more than 5TB in BF16. The harder problem was not training it. It was making it practical to serve. Kimi K3 activates only 104 billion parameters per token, but sparsity alone does not solve the memory and bandwidth bottlenecks. Moonshot redesigned the model across four layers: > LatentMoE compresses tokens before expert routing > KDA keeps a fixed-size attention state > MLA compresses the KV cache for exact retrieval > Native FP4 training cuts the weight footprint Kimi K3 combines three KDA layers with one Gated MLA layer. This gives it constant-memory attention for most layers while retaining full context retrieval where it matters. That hybrid design makes its 1 million token context practical without a KV cache that grows across every token and layer. Quantization-aware training handles the remaining weight problem. Moonshot trains the post-training pipeline in low precision instead of compressing the model after training. Kimi K3 has more than twice the parameters of Kimi K2, but its deployed memory footprint grows by a much smaller ratio.

How do you route across 896 experts without saturating network bandwidth? How do you serve one million tokens without storing hundreds of gigabytes of KV cache? Full breakdown of the architecture that keeps Kimi K3 deployable: alphasignal.ai/news/why-kimi… Link Why Kimi K3's architecture is a masterclass in AI efficiency | AlphaSignal Kimi K3 is a 2.8 trillion parameter multimodal MoE model with only ~104 billion parameters active per token, a 1 million token context window, and ranks third alphasignal.ai

processed.summary: Cette semaine a été riche en annonces et réflexions pour les débutants passionnés d'IA. OpenAI a frappé fort avec son modèle Astra résolvant des problèmes mathématiques complexes, tandis que Google DeepMind a dévoilé Gemini Robotics 2, dotant les robots d'une intelligence corporelle avancée. Les discussions ont également porté sur la sécurité des modèles d'IA, avec des incidents cyber révélés par Anthropic et OpenAI, soulignant l'importance des tests rigoureux. Enfin, de nombreux outils et plateformes ont été mis en avant, montrant comment l'IA peut être utilisée pour la création de mondes virtuels, l'analyse de données, ou l'aide à l'apprentissage.

glossaire.definition: Un modèle de langage étendu est un programme d'IA capable de comprendre, générer et manipuler le langage humain, comme ChatGPT ou Claude.
Un agent IA est un programme capable de réaliser des tâches complexes de manière autonome, en utilisant des outils et en prenant des décisions pour atteindre un objectif.
Un modèle dont les 'poids' (les paramètres internes appris lors de l'entraînement) sont rendus publics, permettant à n'importe qui de l'étudier, de l'améliorer ou de l'utiliser.
Le processus par lequel un modèle d'IA utilise ce qu'il a appris pour faire des prédictions ou générer de nouvelles données, comme une réponse textuelle ou une image.
Désigne un modèle d'IA capable de traiter et de comprendre différents types de données, comme le texte, les images, l'audio et la vidéo, simultanément.
Une technique d'attaque où un utilisateur malveillant manipule le modèle d'IA en insérant des instructions cachées ou conflictuelles dans la conversation, contournant ses mesures de sécurité.

highlights.text_fr: Nous commençons à quitter le territoire où l'on testerait un LLM en lui demandant par exemple de « créer un SVG d'un pélican à vélo ». Comme idée pour généraliser cela, j'étais curieux de voir ce que ferait Opus 5 si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget de 1 million de jetons (~10 $) et lui demandais un rendu en trois.js. Opus a travaillé pendant environ 2 heures et a écrit 5 500 lignes de code qui ont rendu (procéduralement) l'histoire. C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. Mais c'est un peu sidérant que le LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux en coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime tout cela, et qu'il fasse même quelque chose. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne de sensé ne passerait jamais le temps d'écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, c'est donc un exemple où l'on passe de « personne ne ferait jamais ça » à « bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est presque gratuit ». Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé par la création de mondes hyper personnalisés dans lesquels vous pouvez imaginer plonger des joueurs, par exemple ici pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère de X à la demande. Une dernière pensée est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLM : ils ne peuvent pas facilement auditer leur travail car ils ne sont pas capables de percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou de jouer à des jeux. Ici, Opus 5 a dû très lentement et péniblement prendre des captures d'écran à différents moments, et il a fait quelques erreurs et créé pas mal de choses bancales. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, manque encore beaucoup. Vidéo
highlights.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

highlights.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une bonne et longue session de divagation. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en mode /voix et juste divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, tout y passe, un flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare au début, quelque chose comme « passage à la reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe... ». Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont étonnamment bons pour reconstituer de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de votre propre fouillis de pensées ressort de manière assez plus propre que ce avec quoi vous avez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la fusion des esprits et avez moins de choses à corriger à partir de ce moment-là.
highlights.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

tips.text_fr: Une méthode que je trouve utile pour travailler avec les LLM est une bonne et longue session de divagation. Parfois, le LLM a besoin de plus d'informations pour comprendre ce que vous essayez d'accomplir, mais vous êtes trop paresseux pour les taper. Dans ces cas, j'aime m'adosser, passer en mode /voix et juste divaguer pendant environ 10 minutes, un désordre total, tout y passe, un flux de conscience complet. Parfois, je le déclare au début, quelque chose comme « passage à la reconnaissance vocale, désolé pour les fautes de frappe... ». Parfois, j'en fais une petite interview en quelques tours. Mais je trouve que les LLM sont étonnamment bons pour reconstituer de longues divagations incohérentes et souvent leur écho de votre propre fouillis de pensées ressort de manière assez plus propre que ce avec quoi vous avez commencé. Le résultat est que vous améliorez la fusion des esprits et avez moins de choses à corriger à partir de ce moment-là.
tips.text_original: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

idees.text_fr: Nous commençons à quitter le territoire où l'on testerait un LLM en lui demandant par exemple de « créer un SVG d'un pélican à vélo ». Comme idée pour généraliser cela, j'étais curieux de voir ce que ferait Opus 5 si je lui donnais le premier paragraphe du Seigneur des Anneaux, un budget de 1 million de jetons (~10 $) et lui demandais un rendu en trois.js. Opus a travaillé pendant environ 2 heures et a écrit 5 500 lignes de code qui ont rendu (procéduralement) l'histoire. C'est un peu bancal mais amusant. Mais c'est un peu sidérant que le LLM doive placer et orchestrer divers éléments polygonaux en coordonnées (x,y,z) et écrire du code qui anime tout cela, et qu'il fasse même quelque chose. J'aime aussi ce genre d'exemples car personne de sensé ne passerait jamais le temps d'écrire quelque chose d'aussi personnalisé, mais les LLM ont toute l'endurance et la patience du monde, c'est donc un exemple où l'on passe de « personne ne ferait jamais ça » à « bien sûr, pourquoi pas, c'est presque gratuit ». Il pourrait y en avoir beaucoup plus. Mais je suis enthousiasmé par la création de mondes hyper personnalisés dans lesquels vous pouvez imaginer plonger des joueurs, par exemple ici pour participer à l'histoire du Seigneur des Anneaux en tant que PNJ spectateur, ou l'un des personnages, ou etc. Quelque chose comme un GTA éphémère de X à la demande. Une dernière pensée est que le domaine des mondes/jeux expose une faiblesse des LLM : ils ne peuvent pas facilement auditer leur travail car ils ne sont pas capables de percevoir efficacement et nativement des vidéos ou de jouer à des jeux. Ici, Opus 5 a dû très lentement et péniblement prendre des captures d'écran à différents moments, et il a fait quelques erreurs et créé pas mal de choses bancales. Un exemple de capacité brute (multimodale, gameplay) qui, je pense, manque encore beaucoup. Vidéo
idees.text_original: We're starting to leave the territory where you'd test an LLM by e.g. "create an svg of pelican on a bicycle". As one idea to generalize it, I was interested what Opus 5 would do if I gave it the first paragraph of the Lord of the Rings, a 1M token budget (~$10) and asked for three js render of it. Opus went off for ~2 hours and wrote 5500 lines of code that (procedurally) rendered the story. It's kind of janky but fun. But it's a bit mindboggling that the LLM has to place and orchestrate various polygon assets in (x,y,z) coordinates and write code that animates it all, and that it even does anything at all. I also like this kind of examples because no one in their right mind would ever spend the time to write something this custom but LLMs have all the stamina and patience in the world, so it's an example where we go from "no one would ever do this" to "sure, why not, it's ~free". There might be a lot more. But I'm excited about creating hyper custom worlds that you can imagine dropping players into, e.g. here to participate in the LoTR story as a spectator NPC, or one of the characters, or etc. Something like an ephemeral GTA of X on demand. Last thought is that the domain of worlds/games exposes a weakness in LLMs: they can't easily audit their work because they aren't able to efficiently and natively perceive videos or play games within them. Here, Opus 5 had to very slowly and painstakingly take screenshots at different points, and it messed up a few times and created a bunch of jank. An example of raw capability (multimodal, gameplay) that I think is still quite lacking. Video

idees.text_fr: Les mathématiques et l'informatique ont eu une relation très étroite dans certains milieux universitaires. Richard Courant a proposé des méthodes pour résoudre numériquement les équations aux dérivées partielles en 1928. Von Neumann a compris que l'on pouvait utiliser des ordinateurs électroniques pour cela en 1940. Tous deux étaient des mathématiciens. Ces méthodes sont les ancêtres des méthodes par éléments finis, pour lesquelles l'Institut Courant de NYU est célèbre. L'Institut Courant a été créé en 1935 en tant que département de mathématiques de NYU. Il était inhabituel en ce sens qu'il y avait beaucoup de travail sur l'analyse numérique et le calcul scientifique, avec une utilisation intensive de supercalculateurs. En 1952, la Commission de l'énergie atomique a installé un puissant ordinateur électronique à NYU, ce qui a conduit à la création du Courant Mathematics and Computing Laboratory. Le département d'informatique a été créé à partir des mathématiques en 1969 par Jacob T Schwartz. Courant est maintenant une école avec trois départements : mathématiques, informatique et science des données. L'existence continue d'un centre HPC à NYU est un facteur qui a permis à la recherche en IA de décoller.
idees.text_original: Mathematics and computing have had a very tight relationship in some corners of academia. Richard Courant proposed methods to solve PDEs numerically in 1928. Von Neuman figured out you could use electronic computers for it in 1940. Both were mathematicians. These methods are the ancestors of finite element methods, for which NYU's Courant Institute is famous. The Courant Institute was created in 1935 as NYU's mathematics department. It was unusual in that there was a lot of work on numerical analysis and scientific computing, with heavy use of supercomputers. In 1952, the Atomic Energy Commission installed a powerful electronic computer at NYU, which led to the creation of the Courant Mathematics and Computing Laboratory. The computer science department was spun off from mathematics in 1969 by Jacob T Schwartz. Courant is now a school with three departments: mathematics, computer science, and data science. The continued existence of an HPC center at NYU is one factor that enabled AI research to take off.
idees.decryptage: Ce tweet explique l'histoire des liens étroits entre les mathématiques et l'informatique, soulignant comment des institutions comme l'Institut Courant ont joué un rôle clé en fournissant des infrastructures de calcul puissantes (supercalculateurs) qui ont été essentielles au développement de la recherche en IA.

idees.text_original: Adam Thierer had written the landmark book on "Permissionless Innovation." We get the best ideas when we don't have to ask the government in advance for permission to invent. Protecting open source AI is now a critical part of ensuring this. Adam Thierer (@AdamThierer) We stand at a critical crossroads in the debate over AI governance in the United States, and it feels like we are inching closer to a very serious battle over whether or not open source models will even be allowed in an environment where a new de facto licensing regime has been taking shape. Lacking formal congressional statutory frameworks or clear administration rules (like the diffusion rule revision), we appear to be left with a sporadic, arbitrary, non-transparent process for model review. The fiction of “voluntary” agreements hangs over this debate, and some large model developers are already showing an incredible willingness to bend over backwards to accommodate national security-related officials / orders that the rest of us are not privy to. It's a very opaque process. And those model developers are expected to play ball with those officials, or else their models get pulled from the market or held up for long periods. Or they will lose any government procurement contracts they have. There is nothing “voluntary” about it when that Sword of Damocles hangs in the room. As this mess worsens, at some point the question of how to handle open source models will come into sharper focus because it will have to. I've even heard some rumors lately that something may be coming from the admin on this front to address this. Needless to say, if this informal new AI model review regime expands and takes on more pre-vetting characteristics / requirements, it is hard to see how open source players could comply with such quasi-licensing of AI models. Specifically, if this ambiguous new regime is accompanied by a general presumption of ‘restrict-until-permitted,’ then that would spell doom for open source. That is a very dark path for our country. Worse yet, of course, would be a move by national security officials to more directly restrict open source models and capabilities. If that happens, then we would be right back in the thick of a Clipper Chip-like battle along the lines of what we saw in the late 1990s. That is a much darker path for America. Meanwhile, open source developers have no “golden shares” or other goodies to offer the government to make their problems go away. Let’s be clear: If our government takes the dark path, it will become the single most important battle over computational freedom of modern times. It is time for people to make a stand in defense of open source before it is too late. — https://nitter.net/AdamThierer/status/2075237102099251371#m

idees.text_fr: Pour aborder les limites du deep learning et éviter un blocage, le domaine de l'IA a commencé par appliquer le patch (1), qui a commencé à être présenté 9 mois plus tard en décembre 2024 et est maintenant devenu complètement omniprésent. Cela entraînerait probablement des progrès significatifs, mais ce n'est pas la solution ultime, plus une amélioration incrémentale. 2. Changer le mécanisme d'entraînement pour quelque chose de plus robuste que le SGD, comme le principe MDL. Cela nécessiterait pratiquement de s'éloigner complètement du deep learning (ajustement de courbe) et d'adopter la recherche de programmes discrets à la place (ce que j'ai préconisé pendant de nombreuses années comme moyen de s'attaquer aux problèmes de raisonnement...) — https://nitter.net/fchollet/status/1766044732830999014#m

Oui, cela semble relativement compliqué, mais c'est essentiellement une version de production à grande échelle de leur modèle Kimi Linear sorti l'année dernière (passant de 48 milliards à 2,8 trillions ; K3 est de loin le plus grand modèle open-weight actuellement) 2. Le seul nouveau composant par rapport à Kimi Linear est le LatentMoE. Je l'ai omis dans la figure ci-dessous car elle est déjà très chargée, mais c'est essentiellement le même LatentMoE que dans Nemotron 3 Ultra (vous pouvez le trouver dans ma Galerie d'architectures LLM si vous êtes curieux). L'idée ici est de compresser (projeter vers le bas) de grandes couches linéaires, de manière similaire à l'attention latente multi-tête. 3. La tendance générale de Kimi K3 (similaire à Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4 et d'autres) est également vers une meilleure efficacité d'inférence. C'est-à-dire qu'il existe de nombreux composants qui remplacent les composants existants par des versions optimisées en efficacité. C'est-à-dire MoE -> LatentMoE, attention régulière -> attention latente multi-tête et Kimi Delta Attention. (J'ai également de courts tutoriels et des articles dans ma galerie si vous êtes curieux de plus de détails). 4. Le seul changement de composant qui n'est pas une optimisation d'efficacité est les résidus d'attention. Comme DeepSeek V4 a amélioré le chemin résiduel avec mHC (Hyper-Connexions à contrainte de variété), les résidus d'attention sont un moyen d'améliorer le chemin résiduel, mais cela fonctionne un peu différemment. C'est-à-dire que mHC a élargi le chemin résiduel. Les résidus d'attention (également déjà présents dans Kimi Linear) connectent les résidus entre les couches ; la connexion elle-même utilise un score d'attention pour un poids d'importance/contribution. Selon le rapport, cela améliore la perte de validation et les performances en aval (un peu) de manière constante et ajoute environ 4 % au coût d'entraînement et 2 % au coût d'inférence. 5. Fait intéressant, Kimi K3 s'est débarrassé de toutes les couches RoPE et utilise NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) partout à la place. (Encore une fois, cela est hérité de Kimi Linear). Dans d'autres architectures, la tendance récente était vers RoPE dans les couches d'attention locales (comme l'attention à fenêtre glissante) et NoPE dans les couches globales. Il y avait quelques architectures qui n'utilisaient NoPE que partout, mais c'est la première de niveau 'frontier' à ma connaissance. 6. Kimi K3 a maintenant également un support multimodal natif, ce qui est excellent ! Il y a plusieurs autres détails d'entraînement intéressants dans le rapport technique, mais c'est tout pour le front de l'architecture pour le moment. Une très belle publication dans l'ensemble.
idees.text_original: The Kimi K3 architecture figure for yesterday's big open-weight model release, along with some observations and thoughts. 1. Yes, it looks relatively complicated, but it's essentially a scaled-up production version of their Kimi Linear model they released last year (scaled up from 48B -> 2.8T; K3 is by far the biggest open-weight model right now) 2. The one new component compared to Kimi Linear is the LatentMoE. I omitted it in the figure below since it's already very crowded, but that's essentially the same LatentMoE as in Nemotron 3 Ultra (you can find it in my LLM Architecture Gallery if you are curious). The idea here is to compress (down-project) large linear layers similar to multi-head latent attention. 3. Kimi K3's overall trend (similar to Nemotron 3, DeepSeek V4, and others) is also towards better inference efficiency. That is, there are many components that replace existing components with efficiency-tweaked versions. I.e., MoE -> LatentMoE, regular attention -> multi-head latent attention and Kimi Delta Attention. (I also have short tutorials and write-ups in my gallery if you are curious about additional details). 4. The one component change that is not an efficiency tweak is attention residuals. Like DeepSeek V4 improved the residual path with mHC (manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections), attention residuals are a way to improve the residual path, but it works a bit differently. I.e., mHC made the residual path wider. Attention residuals (also already part of Kimi Linear) connect the residuals across layers; the connection itself uses an attention score for an important/contribution weight. According to the report, it improves the validation loss and downstream performance (a bit) consistently and adds about 4% in training cost and 2% in inference cost. 5. Interestingly, Kimi K3 got rid of all RoPE layers and uses NoPE (No Positional Embeddings) everywhere instead. (Again, this is inherited from Kimi Linear). In other architectures, the recent trend was towards RoPE in local attention layers (like sliding window attention) and NoPE in the global layers. There were a few architectures that only used NoPE everywhere, but this is the first frontier-level one as far as I know. 6. Kimi K3 now also has native multimodal support, which is great! There are several other interesting training tidbits in the technical report, but that's it from the architecture front so far. A really great release overall.

Google a eu la première recherche approfondie et a pivoté rapidement avec Bard.
idees.text_original: Given today, it is surprising how daring Microsoft & Google were initially with AI. Microsoft released GPT-4 before OpenAI, didn't back down after Sydney & got Copilot to market quickly (the 1st professional AI tool) Google had the first deep research & pivoted fast with Bard.
idees.decryptage: Ce tweet souligne que Microsoft et Google ont pris des risques importants et ont été très audacieux au début de l'ère de l'IA (avec GPT-4, Copilot et Bard), ce qui est surprenant au vu des inquiétudes actuelles concernant la prudence dans le développement de l'IA.

idees.text_fr: Les deux entreprises ont pris d'énormes risques de réputation sur une technologie naissante avant même qu'il n'y ait un marché (Bard était imprécis et avait une génération d'images controversée, Sydney était insensé). Leur incapacité à être audacieux maintenant, alors que le marché est plus clair, est d'autant plus surprenante.
idees.text_original: Both companies took tremendous reputational risks on an early technology before there was even a market for it (Bard was inaccurate and had controversial imagegen, Sydney was insane). Their inability to be daring now, when the market is clearer, is more surprising as a result.

idees.text_fr: Sur l'IA qui prend des emplois : Un agriculteur d'il y a 50 ans dirait que votre travail aujourd'hui n'est pas un vrai travail. Quand j'ai interviewé Sam Altman il y a quelques mois, voici comment il a expliqué l'avenir du travail : « Non seulement ils ne vous croiraient pas que cette chose allait arriver, mais ils regarderaient très probablement ce que vous ou moi faisons et diraient que ce n'est pas un vrai travail. » « Si vous cultivez... vous gardez les gens en vie. Et vous, les gens du futur -- la vie est devenue trop facile pour vous... vous jouez à un jeu pour remplir votre temps et votre besoin de vous sentir important. » « Pour nous, cependant, cela semble réel. Certainement, pour moi, cela semble réel. » « Si nous pouvions voir ces emplois du futur, nous dirions : d'accord, peut-être que nos emplois n'étaient pas aussi réels que celui d'un agriculteur, mais c'est beaucoup plus réel que ce jeu auquel vous jouez pour vous divertir. » « J'ai quelques inquiétudes à court terme alors que nous traversons cette transition, mais je suis tellement prêt à parier sur les pulsions humaines telles qu'elles sont. Je pense que nous trouverons beaucoup de choses à faire. » Vidéo
idees.text_original: On AI taking jobs: A farmer from 50 years ago would say your job today isn't real work. When I interviewed Sam Altman a few months back, this was how he explained the future of work: "Not only would they not believe you that this thing was gonna happen, they very likely would look at what you do or I do and say, that's not real work." "If you're farming... you're keeping people alive. And you people of the future -- life just got too easy for you... you're playing a game to fill your time and your need to feel important." "To us, though, it feels real. Certainly, to me it feels real." "If we could see those jobs of the future, we would be like: okay, maybe our jobs were not as real as a farmer's job, but it's a lot more real than this game you're playing to entertain yourself." "I have some short-term worries as we go through this transition, but I'm so willing to bet on human drives being what they are. I think we'll find plenty of things to do." Video
idees.decryptage: Ce tweet présente l'opinion de Sam Altman, PDG d'OpenAI, sur l'évolution des emplois avec l'IA. Il suggère que notre perception du "vrai travail" change avec le temps, et que de nouveaux types d'emplois, actuellement inimaginables, émergeront grâce à l'IA, répondant aux besoins humains fondamentaux d'activité et d'importance.

Lorsqu'un modèle génère du texte, une grande partie du temps est consacrée à déplacer ses poids de la mémoire vers les unités de calcul. outils.text_original: New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez , @duerr_seb , and @MilksandMatcha . When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units. Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents. Skills you'll gain: - Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck - Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals - Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively My teams use Cerebras for several applications that are latency sensitive.
